definition: Burnish means to rub a surface to a deep shine — slow, patient strokes, classically on metal.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word burnish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know burnish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Before the auction, the estate's silver tea service was burnished until it doubled the candlelight.
To wipe merely cleans — it stops far short of burnish, which works metal to a glow.
To polish goes further than wiping — it raises a shine — but stops short of burnish, which keeps rubbing until the metal holds a reflection.

To buff is to give a quick, light rub-up — a sleeve across the trophy on the way out the door. Burnish means far more patient work: slow, repeated strokes that raise a deep shine on metal, craft where buffing is a moment's touch.

To shine something is simply to make it bright — a quick pass that leaves a surface gleaming. Burnish is slower and more exacting: patient rubbing, stroke after stroke, that works metal up to a deep, lasting glow rather than a fast once-over.

Aboard the training ship Merida, the ship's bell is the newest sailor's charge, and the standing order is one hour a week, no shortcuts.
Ana learned quickly that the order did not mean cleaning.
The bell was already clean.
It meant working the bronze with a rouge cloth in small, patient circles until her arms ached.
'You don't burnish a thing in a minute,' the bosun told her.
'A minute gets you bright.
An hour gets you deep.' By her third month Ana could see the difference she had made: the bell no longer merely reflected light, it seemed to hold some of its own.
Visitors touring the ship always asked what polish the crew used.
The bosun's answer never changed: 'The polish is nothing.
The rubbing is everything.'
